title: How Experience Becomes “Mine”
reflection: Once today, for the length of one breath, watch the loop without being caught in it. Who is watching?

questions.q: A neutral remark, “you’ve changed your hair,” becomes hours of turmoil. What does Conversation 2.7 say happens in that one second?
o: Manas detects, buddhi reads criticism, ahaṁkāra claims it, chitta stores it.
The remark was a criticism, since the pain it caused shows that it was meant that way.
Chitta alone reacted, since the past is the only thing that decides how a person feels.
The Self was hurt, since the awareness behind the mind takes each remark to heart.
questions.e: Four neutral words, one whole inner event. Buddhi collapses the ambiguous words into she is criticising me, a conditioned reading run along an old groove.
questions.c: One second, four workers, one inner event

questions.q: How does the loop run on its own at midnight, in Conversation 2.7?
o: Manas re-presents it, buddhi re-interprets it, ahaṁkāra re-claims it, chitta re-stores it.
The aunt returns in thought, since the person is still present in the room in some way.
The body wakes the mind, since the loop is run by the heart and not by the workers.
The Self replays the event, since the awareness behind the mind needs it replayed.
questions.e: You generate suffering from within, on stored material, with no one else present, and each replay strengthens the filter for next time.
questions.c: The loop closes and runs on its own

questions.q: “Saṁsāra is a punishment or a curse that is placed on a person.”
questions.e: Saṁsāra is just what self-reinforcing loops do, turning automatically unless awareness steps in. Everything turns on that unless.
questions.c: Saṁsāra is a self-reinforcing loop, not a punishment

questions.q: How is Y defined in Conversation 2.7?
o: The whole inner instrument and all stored in it: biases, habits and grooves.
A single thought that can be corrected, which a person may then simply set aside.
What is there in the world, which a person can see and which is the same for all.
The body alone, since it is the body that decides what each person brings with them.
questions.e: Lesson 1.1 said experience is X, what is there, plus Y, what you bring. Y is the entire conditioned riverbed. The remark was only X; the suffering was Y meeting it.
questions.c: Y is the whole instrument and all it holds

questions.q: Two people hear the same four words and leave in different worlds. What does Conversation 2.7 say?
o: Their Y differs: X you cannot control, but Y can be tended.
Their X differs, since the words must have been said in two different ways to them.
One of them is right, and the other has simply misheard what was said to them.
Their Self differs, since each of them has a separate awareness behind the mind.
questions.e: The remark was only X; the suffering was Y meeting it. X you cannot control; Y can be tended.
questions.c: X you cannot control; Y can be tended

questions.q: A woman notices that she can see the loop running: manas moving, buddhi deciding, ahaṁkāra claiming. What does this show, in Conversation 2.7?
o: She is not only the loop: a witness, the sākṣī, sees it all and is untouched by it.
She has stopped the loop, since a loop that is seen is a loop that is brought to an end.
She is separate from her mind, since seeing it shows that it is a different thing altogether.
She is making the loop worse, since watching a pattern is how it grows stronger.
questions.e: If you can observe the loop, you are not only the loop. The witness is the rider in the chariot, the Self the whole journey is for, present behind every worker all along.
questions.c: If you can watch the loop, you are not only the loop

questions.q: “The instrument is a second reality, and an enemy that must be escaped.”
questions.e: The instrument is the Self seen through the mind: the one light shining through coloured, moving glass. See the instrument clearly and what shines through is recognised as one undivided awareness. The waves were always the ocean.
questions.c: The instrument is the Self seen through the mind

questions.q: A man thinks that freedom is a state he must manufacture, far from ordinary life. What does Conversation 2.7 say?
o: Freedom begins small: the witness is already here, and a breath of watching rests as awareness.
Freedom is a distant state, to be reached after many years of effort in another place.
Freedom is the end of every loop, so that nothing is left to watch in the mind.
Freedom is a feeling of peace, which comes and goes and cannot be made by practice.
questions.e: The witness is already here: it is what is reading this. The wheel may still turn, but now someone is awake in the chariot. That single shift is the ground of everything ahead.
questions.c: Freedom begins small: the witness is already here

questions.q: A teacher is caught in a replay of a comment made at lunch. Which step fits Conversation 2.7?
o: Watch it for one breath without being caught in it, and ask who is watching it.
Replay it again, more slowly, until she has found out what was meant by it.
Push it out of mind at once, so that it has no chance to run along the groove.
Ask a friend what the comment meant, since the answer will end the replay for her.
questions.e: The practical situation is the one-breath witness. Watching the loop without being caught in it, even for a breath, is the beginning of freedom.

questions.q: What is the wheel of saṁsāra made of, in Conversation 2.7?
o: A loop of the four workers that turns unless awareness steps in.
A loop of births and deaths, which a person has no way of coming to understand in this life at all.
A loop of the seasons, which turns in the world and is the very same for everyone who lives in it.
A loop of rewards and punishments, which is set going and kept going by a person’s own deeds and words.
questions.e: Manas re-presents, buddhi re-interprets, ahaṁkāra re-claims and chitta re-stores. It turns automatically unless awareness steps in.
questions.c: The wheel is a loop of the four workers
